steps.premise: Learners may be unsure whether an opponent welcomes spoken questions.
steps.action: Set aside a couple of tables where players expect questions during play.
steps.consequence: A learner there can ask about a move with confidence.
steps.quote: Keep a couple of tables for games where spoken questions are welcome, so a learner can ask about a move without guessing whether their opponent minds.

steps.premise: A demonstration beside an active board can draw a crowd around that match.
steps.action: Place a teaching board in a corner away from games.
steps.consequence: A helper can demonstrate a position with space for interested visitors.
steps.quote: Place a demonstration board in a corner away from active games, giving a helper room to show a position without gathering a crowd around someone else's match.

steps.premise: An unsolicited suggestion can give away a move a newcomer could work out.
steps.action: Ask spectators to wait until players invite suggestions.
steps.consequence: The newcomer has time to think through the position independently.
steps.quote: Ask spectators to save suggestions until the players invite them, so a newcomer gets the chance to work out a difficult move for themselves.

steps.premise: Some pieces make a clacking noise when placed on a board.
steps.action: Give those pieces felt bases.
steps.consequence: Ordinary play makes less noise throughout a busy room.
steps.quote: Put felt under the pieces that land with a clack. A small change to the sets can quiet a busy room without asking anyone to tiptoe.

steps.premise: A clock sounding at the end of a game can distract nearby players.
steps.action: Mute the beeps on the room's shared clocks.
steps.consequence: Neighbors can keep concentrating when another game ends.
steps.quote: Silence the beeps on communal clocks so the end of one game doesn't break a neighboring player's concentration.

steps.premise: A beginner may need time to decide whether a move is legal.
steps.action: Keep some boards for games with no clock.
steps.consequence: Learners at those boards can think through moves at their own pace.
steps.quote: Keep a few boards available for play without a clock, allowing someone who is still thinking through legal moves to take their time.

steps.premise: Two beginners might need help setting up a board.
steps.action: Include a picture of the initial arrangement with every set.
steps.consequence: They can start a game together without calling across the room.
steps.quote: Give each set a picture of the starting position so two beginners can get going together without having to call across the room for help.

steps.premise: A visitor may be unsure whether a stranger wants a game.
steps.action: Provide a sign the seated player can face toward the entrance whenever they want an opponent.
steps.consequence: An arriving visitor can see the invitation to join.
steps.quote: Offer a small sign that a seated player can turn toward the door when they'd welcome an opponent, taking the guesswork out of joining a stranger.

steps.premise: Visitors waiting at busy times might hover over games that seem close to ending.
steps.action: Keep a written queue while the room is busy.
steps.consequence: Those waiting can sit down to read and keep their place.
steps.quote: Keep a written waiting list during busy periods, letting visitors sit down to read instead of hovering over games that look nearly finished.

steps.premise: A promotion or a piece missing from a set can trigger a search.
steps.action: Store spare queens and other pieces in a clearly findable drawer.
steps.consequence: Players can obtain the piece they need without involving the room.
steps.quote: Put spare queens and other pieces in an easy-to-find drawer, so a promotion or a missing knight doesn't set off a room-wide search.

steps.premise: A tight exit route forces people to squeeze between a board and its player.
steps.action: Space tables to leave a route behind occupied chairs.
steps.consequence: Visitors can reach the exit without cutting through a game.
steps.quote: Arrange the tables so visitors heading for the exit can pass behind seated players without squeezing between a chair and its board.

steps.premise: New arrivals may need an introduction while games are under way.
steps.action: Have a host welcome and quietly orient them just inside the entrance.
steps.consequence: Newcomers learn how the room works without disrupting play.
steps.quote: Ask a host to greet newcomers just inside the door, where a quiet explanation of the room can happen without interrupting a game.

steps.premise: A visitor waiting for an opponent may have nothing to do except watch a game up close.
steps.action: Put a few puzzles based on individual positions on a side desk.
steps.consequence: The visitor can enjoy chess independently while waiting.
steps.quote: Leave a few single-position puzzles on a side desk so someone waiting for an opponent can enjoy chess without watching over a player's shoulder.

steps.premise: A missed check can lead to disagreement over reversing a move.
steps.action: Have the two opponents agree on takebacks before the game begins.
steps.consequence: They have already settled the rule when a mistake occurs.
steps.quote: Invite both players to agree before starting whether they'll allow takebacks, heading off a dispute the first time someone overlooks a check.

steps.premise: Bags in the walkway lead to requests for players to move them.
steps.action: Use hooks or a shelf for bags away from the boards.
steps.consequence: Seated players can play without repeated interruptions over belongings.
steps.quote: Keep bags on hooks or a shelf away from the boards, saving seated players from repeated requests to move their belongings out of a walkway.

steps.premise: Children exploring piece movement need pieces to practise with.
steps.action: Provide a separate set to children who want to practise.
steps.consequence: They can try moves without taking pieces out of an ongoing match.
steps.quote: Give children who want to practise piece movement a set of their own, so they can explore how a knight jumps without borrowing from a live game.

steps.premise: Conversation about a finished match can be lively and last longer than the game.
steps.action: Provide space for analysis away from boards reserved for quiet play.
steps.consequence: Players can carry on their discussion while the quiet games proceed nearby.
steps.quote: Set up a place for post-game discussion a little away from the quiet boards, since a lively analysis can last much longer than the game itself.

steps.premise: A rules disagreement could draw other people into the argument.
steps.action: Encourage players to speak quietly with the host when one arises.
steps.consequence: They have a way to settle it without involving the whole room.
steps.quote: Encourage a quiet word with the host if a disagreement develops, giving players a way to settle a rules question without drawing in the whole room.

steps.premise: Scraping chair legs can startle concentrating players.
steps.action: Put pads on the legs of the noisy chairs.
steps.consequence: People can arrive or leave more quietly.
steps.quote: Fit pads to the chair legs that scrape against the floor, making it easier to come and go without startling people deep in thought.

steps.premise: Learners may want to visit when someone is available and expects to teach.
steps.action: Let them know when the volunteer can teach.
steps.consequence: They can choose a time when they feel comfortable seeking help.
steps.quote: Let learners know when a volunteer will be free to teach, so they can plan a visit when asking for help feels expected.

steps.premise: A visitor might walk through the games simply to see how busy the room is.
steps.action: Keep the tables visible from the entrance.
steps.consequence: They can gauge occupancy before entering the playing area.
steps.quote: Keep the sightline from the entrance to the tables open, allowing visitors to see whether the room is busy before walking through the playing area.

steps.premise: A caller needs somewhere they can use a normal speaking voice.
steps.action: Ask callers to take the conversation in the hallway while the people at their board keep the position.
steps.consequence: The call can proceed outside the room and the game stays ready to resume.
steps.quote: Ask anyone taking a call to step into the hallway, where they can speak normally while the people at their board hold the position.

steps.premise: A beginner may misjudge how long the remaining game will take.
steps.action: Quietly give players advance notice that the room is closing.
steps.consequence: The beginner and opponent have time to agree where to stop.
steps.quote: Give players a quiet heads-up before closing time so a beginner still learning to judge game length can agree on a stopping point with their opponent.

steps.premise: Keeping an unfinished game set up ties up a board.
steps.action: Make paper and a pencil available so players can record the position.
steps.consequence: Two visitors can pause their game and free the board.
steps.quote: Leave a pencil and paper for recording an unfinished position, allowing two visitors to pause a game without having to keep the board occupied.
